ja.etymology: The affirmative has been recorded as jā in both Old and Middle High German. Duden leaves its deeper origin unresolved. Its long written history is clear even though a further derivation is not.
ja.notes: Do not confuse a plain affirmative answer with unstressed ja used to signal shared knowledge.

ich.etymology: An inherited Germanic personal pronoun, recorded as Old High German ih and Middle High German ich. Duden relates it to Latin ego and Greek egō; those are relatives, not languages from which modern German borrowed the word.

sein.etymology: The modern verb combines historically different stems. Duden records sīn for the infinitive; the family of bin originally concerned becoming or growing, while ist and sint supply another stem. The past was and wāren belongs to the family of wesan, meaning to remain or be present. This mixed history helps explain why the forms differ so much.
sein.notes: This history does not make the modern forms interchangeable: ich bin, du bist and er ist remain distinct.

heute.etymology: Old High German hiut(u), later Middle High German hiute, contracted an older expression hiu tagu, meaning on this day. A short everyday time word thus preserves what was once a longer phrase.

mein.etymology: The possessive goes back to Old and Middle High German mīn. The historical form is an ancestor of the modern possessive; the different modern endings in mein, meine and meinen are chosen by the word that follows.

erste.etymology: The ordinal erste belongs with erst. Duden traces erst through Middle High German ēr(e)st to Old High German ērist, historically a superlative in the family of eher. The modern ordinal takes endings, as in erster Tag.
erste.notes: The historical superlative is not a direction to build a new comparative of modern erste. Duden’s ordinal entry also documents its inflected forms.

tag.etymology: Recorded as Old High German tag and Middle High German tac. Duden suggests, rather than establishes, a connection with a verb meaning to burn, with the proposed sense of the time when the sun shines or burns. The historical forms are firmer evidence than that deeper explanation.
tag.notes: The masculine noun for a day is separate from the modern English loanword das Tag for a label.

hier.etymology: Recorded as Old High German hiar and Middle High German hie(r). Duden connects it with the demonstrative stem discussed under her. Its history belongs to pointing out a location, not to a modern compound made by cutting hier into smaller German words.

der.etymology: The definite article was originally a demonstrative, a word pointing out a particular person or thing. Duden records Old and Middle High German der, diu and daʒ. Today its different forms mark case, gender and number; die in this lesson is plural.

history.meaning: demonstrative forms; ancestors of the definite article

andere.etymology: Old and Middle High German ander lies behind the modern forms andere, anderer and anderes. Duden describes the older word as a comparative formation. The lesson’s die anderen uses it for the other people, rather than for a named item that follows.

kennen.etymology: Middle High German kennen meant to know or recognize. An older related form appears as -chennan in Old High German compounds. Duden connects the formation with können in its older sense of knowing or understanding, with an earlier causative sense concerning making something understood.
kennen.notes: Modern kennen and können are different verbs: familiarity is not the same as ability.

noch.etymology: For the temporal adverb, Duden traces Middle High German noch to Old High German noh, combining nu with a small element -h that meant also or and. Its earlier sense concerned now as well. The present phrase noch nicht means not yet.
noch.notes: Duden gives a separate historical explanation for the conjunction noch in weder … noch. That conjunction is not the temporal use in this lesson.

nicht.etymology: Old High German niwiht combined a negative element with wiht, something or a thing. It developed into Middle High German niht and modern nicht. A strengthened expression meaning not anything became the ordinary German negative.
nicht.notes: The modern word is learned as a single negative marker, not assembled from those historical parts in conversation.

so.etymology: Duden records Old and Middle High German sō, originally an adverb meaning in this way. Modern so retains that manner use and also marks degree, as in nicht so gut.

gut.etymology: Old and Middle High German guot originally described something fitting into a structure or arrangement. Duden relates the family to Gatter and Gitter. The everyday sense developed around suitability and goodness; the lesson uses the same word adverbially for knowing people well.

aber.etymology: Duden records Old and Middle High German aber and aver, with older senses of further away, later or again. The modern contrasting conjunction is one later use of this historically wider word. In the lesson it turns from unfamiliar colleagues to Titus’s actual reason for working.

um.etymology: The older spatial word is recorded as Old High German umbi and Middle High German umbe, concerning being around or on both sides. Modern German also uses um with a following zu-marked action to express purpose. In that construction, translating this word as around would give the wrong meaning.
um.notes: The spatial word history is documented by Duden’s preposition entry; the purpose construction is documented separately by its um conjunction entry. No particular date for the change to purpose is asserted.

freund.etymology: Old High German friunt and Middle High German vriunt are the earlier forms. Duden gives the older meaning as a person who loves, connecting the word with the family of frei. The everyday modern noun names a friend; a singular possessive phrase can also describe a romantic partner.

zu.etymology: Older forms of the word include Old High German zuo, za and zi, followed by Middle High German zuo and ze. Modern German has several distinct uses of zu. Here it marks the final action in a purpose construction; it does not mean a destination or require a dative noun.
zu.notes: Duden’s preposition entry supplies the older word forms. Its separate conjunction entry documents the infinitive construction; the lesson distinguishes these modern uses rather than assigning the preposition’s case rule to the infinitive marker.

finden.etymology: Old High German findan became Middle High German vinden. Duden gives the older sense as stepping onto something or coming upon it. Modern finden covers finding things or people; Freunde finden is the usual German combination corresponding to making friends.

geld.etymology: Old High German gelt referred to payment, wages or recompense. Middle High German gelt also covered income and value; the sense of coined payment developed from that family of meanings. Duden connects it with gelten. The modern mass noun normally means money, while Gelder names particular funds or sums.

verdienen.etymology: Duden records Old High German ferdionōn and Middle High German verdienen. The modern verb retains earning as one sense and deserving as another. Its unstressed initial ver- is part of the word, and the participle is verdient rather than a form beginning with ge-.
verdienen.notes: The conjugation is independently documented in Duden: verdient, verdiente, hat verdient.

tschüss.etymology: Duden relates the farewell family to older atschüs and Low German adjüs. It tentatively connects that line with Spanish adiós and ultimately Latin ad deum, an expression directed to God. The proposed borrowing route is marked as probable, not certain; modern tschüss is simply an informal goodbye.
tschüss.notes: The consulted entry is the nominalized greeting Tschüs and explicitly lists Tschüss as a related form. The lesson uses the farewell as an interjection, not as a noun.

titus.etymology: Titus is an ancient Latin personal name. The Dictionary of Medieval Names from European Sources describes its origin as obscure; an attractive modern meaning should not be invented for it. Here it is simply the new employee’s first name.

history.meaning: a personal name of obscure origin

sources.title: Dictionary of Medieval Names from European Sources: Titus

titus.notes: A personal name, not a German common noun. No claim that it means honour, hero or another everyday word.
